title: The Bowl by the Door. One Year of Taking Pocket Change Seriously
body: The experiment ran for a full year and required one purchase. A bowl. It sits by the door, next to the keys, and the rule is shorter than most laws. Coins come off your person at the door, into the bowl, no exceptions, no raids. Four times a year we emptied it, counted it, and spent it on something no budget line would ever have approved. This report is the ledger, because a money habit without numbers is just a sermon. The quarterly counts, stated plainly. First quarter, the equivalent of sixty-one units; second, seventy-four; third, fifty-eight; fourth, ninety-two, inflated by December, when guests pay cash for help they could have had for free and the bowl collects the change of a whole neighborhood's kindness. Year total. Two hundred and eighty-five units of small coins that, under the previous regime, lived in jacket pockets, car cupholders, and the washing machine's secret economy, where they circulated in and out of usefulness without ever being anyone's. What it funded, chosen by household vote at each emptying. A proper replacement for the kitchen timer that had been estimating rather than timing; one month of the good coffee, the kind we call library coffee because we drink it while reading; and a fund contribution toward a repair we had been postponing. None of these were purchases the budget could not make. All of them were purchases the budget never made, because the budget speaks in large round numbers and this bowl speaks in the exact currency of indifference, the coins too small to matter individually and, banked, plenty. The behavioral findings matter more than the sums. First. The door is the right place. Wallets empty where hands are already busy; the bowl rides the existing ritual of keys, so the habit attached itself in about four days with zero willpower spent after. Second. Cash did not disappear from our lives the way reports keep promising; it thinned to a trickle of specific moments, markets, tips, favors, and the bowl caught that trickle completely. Third, and this surprised me. The bowl changed how we spend in a wider way. Once coins had a visible destination, the casualness about small amounts became harder to maintain in other categories. A subscription nobody uses now looks like the bowl's coins leaving through a different door. Small money, made visible, audits big money. The honest costs and failures, so you can replicate with clear eyes. We raided the bowl exactly once, in March, for a parking meter, and the raid was repaid with interest within the week, because a rule that cannot survive one raid was never a rule, just theater. The counting takes about twenty minutes quarterly and is, unexpectedly, a decent family event, silver in stacks, arguments about whose coins were whose, a spreadsheet updated with ceremony. And there is one genuine loss. The washing machine has gone quiet. We miss it more than we expected. If your house has a jar, a drawer, or a hedge of coins on every horizontal surface, promote one of them to the door. One bowl, one rule, one quarterly count. Two hundred and eighty-five units of found money this year says the smallest denomination in your economy has been waiting for a job, and the door is where it has always wanted to work.
